sections.skill: Use explanations as a starting point and review code against requirements

questions.prompt: How should you treat a tool's explanation of code?

choices.text: As a replacement for running it
As a starting point to check
As proof of what the code does

questions.correct_answer: As a starting point to check
questions.intro: Tools can EXPLAIN code in plain words, which is helpful for learning. Treat an explanation as a STARTING POINT: it may describe what code was meant to do rather than what it does. A CODE REVIEW checks code LINE BY LINE against its REQUIREMENTS. For each line ask: What does it do? Is it needed? Does it match the requirement? Is anything missing? Comments, names and explanations can all be wrong, so check the actual statements. Example: a comment says "return the largest number," but the code uses min(), which returns the smallest.

sections.skill: Compare reviewing code with proofreading a recipe

questions.prompt: Why not stop at the recipe title?

choices.text: It says what it should be, not what the lines do
Because titles of recipes are always wrong

questions.correct_answer: It says what it should be, not what the lines do
questions.intro: When you proofread a recipe for a friend, you do not just read the title ("Easy Chocolate Cake") and say "looks good." You check each line: is it "1 cup sugar" or "1 tablespoon"? Is the oven temperature there? Did they forget the eggs? The title is like a code comment: it tells you what it is supposed to be. The lines tell you what will actually happen. Code review is proofreading each line against what the code should do.

sections.title: Apply it

sections.skill: Review for what is missing and keep changes reviewable

questions.prompt: Code divides by the number of items but never checks for zero items. What kind of finding is this?
questions.intro: A good review also looks for what is NOT there: a missing check for empty input, a requirement that was skipped, or an unhandled error. Large changes are hard to review well; ask for small changes you can read in full. If you cannot understand a part of the code, that is a finding: ask for a simpler version or an explanation you can verify by running small examples, rather than approving it.
